caption_hook: Delaware may be the lowest state, but its rocks run from ice-age sand to a billion-year-old gneiss.

layers.name: COLUMBIA FORMATION
layers.what: During the Ice Age, rivers and rising and falling seas spread sand and gravel across the coastal plain. That thin blanket is the ground under most of Delaware.
layers.bonus: Delaware's high point, Ebright Azimuth, is just 448 ft: the lowest high point of any state.

layers.name: CALVERT FORMATION
layers.what: A shallow Miocene sea once covered central Delaware. Its sands hold fossil whales, sharks and shellfish, plus a few land animals washed in from nearby shores.
layers.bonus: At Pollack Farm in Kent County, a dig 17 million years deep found Delaware's first land-mammal fossils.

layers.name: POTOMAC FORMATION
layers.what: Rivers from the rising Appalachians spread clay and sand across the land in the dinosaur age. It is the oldest sediment layer of Delaware's coastal plain.
layers.bonus: It holds scattered lignite, a soft, young kind of coal that never fully matured.

layers.name: WILMINGTON COMPLEX
layers.what: A chain of volcanic islands in an ancient ocean crashed into North America and was welded on. Its dark, baked rocks now underlie the hills around Wilmington.
layers.bonus: The Brandywine Creek valley cuts straight through these ancient volcanic roots.

layers.name: BALTIMORE GNEISS
layers.what: In the northwest corner, banded gneiss from deep inside an ancient mountain chain pokes through. It is the only Precambrian rock unit in Delaware's Piedmont.
layers.bonus: Its age, about 1.1 billion years, is nearly a quarter of the Earth's entire history.
